lessons.title: Principles of Wheat Cleaning
lessons.body:
Wheat arrives at the mill with more than just grain. It carries stones, sand, straw, chaff, weed seeds, broken kernels, and sometimes metal or glass. If these impurities go into the mill, they damage equipment, wear out rolls, and end up in your flour. Cleaning is not optionalâit is the first step to safe, quality flour. In Africa, wheat is often harvested by hand or small combines, so it may contain more foreign matter than wheat from large farms. Your job is to remove everything that is not wheat.

The cleaning process uses differences in size, shape, density, and magnetic properties. Screens separate by size: small holes let sand fall through, large holes let bigger trash stay on top. Aspirators use air to lift light materials like chaff and dust. Destoners use a vibrating deck and air to separate heavy stones from wheat. Magnetic separators catch iron pieces like nails or wire. Each machine targets a specific impurity.

Start by taking a sample of incoming wheat. Weigh 1 kg and hand-pick all foreign matter. If impurities are more than 2% by weight, you need extra cleaning steps. Common weeds in Africa include wild oats, corn cockle, and ryegrass. These are similar in size to wheat, so they need specific screens or gravity separators. Also check for moisture: if wheat is above 14% moisture, it may clog screens. Dry it to below 13% before cleaning.

A typical cleaning flow in a small African mill: receiving pit â coarse screen (removes straw, sticks) â aspirator (removes dust, chaff) â destoner (removes stones) â magnetic separator (removes metal) â fine screen (removes small seeds) â to tempering. You can combine machines, but never skip the destonerâstones break millstones and roller mills. Inspect screens daily for holes or wear. Replace torn screens immediately.

Keep records: how much wheat you cleaned, how much waste removed, and what types of impurities. This helps you adjust settings and train staff. Clean wheat means better flour yield, less downtime, and happier customers. Remember: cleaning protects your mill and your reputation.

lessons.title: Cleaning Equipment: Separators, Aspirators, and Destoners
lessons.body:
To clean wheat well, you need the right machines. This lesson covers three essential types: separators, aspirators, and destoners. They work together to remove different impurities. You can buy them new or build simple versions locally. Many African mills start with a rotary screen separator, a simple aspirator, and a gravity destoner.

Separators use screens to sort by size. A common type is the rotary drum separator: a rotating cylinder with holes. Wheat falls through holes; larger trash stays inside and exits at the end. For small seeds like wild oats, use a screen with holes slightly smaller than wheatâwheat stays on top, seeds fall through. In Africa, you can make a vibrating screen with a motor and eccentric weight. Set the screen at a 10â15 degree slope. Feed wheat at a steady rateâabout 1 ton per hour per meter of screen width. Shake vigorously to keep holes clear.

Aspirators use air to lift light materials. A simple aspirator is a vertical pipe with an upward air stream. Wheat falls down; chaff, dust, and light seeds are blown up and out. Adjust air speed: too slow and trash stays; too fast and good wheat is blown away. Test by catching output: you want trash up, wheat down. For a 1-ton/hour flow, use a fan moving about 10â15 cubic meters of air per minute. In dusty African conditions, clean the air filter daily.

Destoners separate by density. A destoner is a vibrating deck with a porous surface. Air blows up through the deck. Heavy stones stay on the deck and move uphill; lighter wheat floats and moves downhill. Set the deck angle at 5â10 degrees and vibration speed at 300â500 strokes per minute. Feed wheat evenly. If stones carry over with wheat, increase air flow or reduce feed rate. If wheat goes with stones, reduce air flow or increase deck angle. Check the stone discharge every hourâstones should be dry and free of wheat.

Maintain equipment: grease bearings weekly, check belts and screens daily, and keep motors dry. In humid African climates, rust is a problemâpaint steel parts and store spare screens indoors. Train operators to listen for unusual noises and stop the machine if something breaks. A well-maintained cleaner saves money and produces better flour.

lessons.title: Tempering and Conditioning Methods
lessons.body:
Tempering, also called conditioning, means adding water to wheat and letting it rest before milling. This makes the bran tough and the endosperm soft, so they separate easily during milling. Without tempering, bran shatters into flour, giving dark color and poor baking quality. In Africa, where wheat may be dry and hard, tempering is critical for good flour.

First, know your wheat. Hard wheat (like most bread wheat) needs more water and longer rest than soft wheat. Target moisture: hard wheat 15.5â16.5%, soft wheat 14.5â15.5%. If wheat starts at 10% moisture, you need to add about 5â6% water. For 100 kg wheat, add 5â6 liters of clean water. Use a sprayer or mixing screw to wet wheat evenly. Let it rest in a bin for 12â24 hours for hard wheat, 6â12 hours for soft wheat. In hot African climates, rest time may be shorterâcheck moisture after 6 hours.

There are two main methods: cold tempering and warm tempering. Cold tempering uses room-temperature water. Warm tempering heats water to 40â50Â°C; this speeds water penetration, so rest time drops to 4â8 hours. Warm tempering is useful in cool highland areas like Ethiopia or Kenya. But never exceed 50Â°Câtoo hot and you damage gluten. For small mills, cold tempering is simpler and safer.

Add water in stages if wheat is very dry. First add half the water, mix, rest 2 hours, then add the rest. This prevents surface wetness. Use a moisture meter to check after rest. If moisture is low, add more water and rest another 2 hours. If too wet, mix with dry wheat or let it dry in thin layers.

Conditioning also includes adding heat or steam in large mills, but for African small mills, water alone works. After tempering, wheat should be cool and dry to touch. Mill immediatelyâdo not let tempered wheat sit for days, or it may mold. Record water added, rest time, and final moisture. Adjust next batch based on flour quality. Good tempering gives higher yield, whiter flour, and less energy use in milling.

lessons.title: Moisture Measurement and Control
lessons.body:
Moisture is the most important number in wheat cleaning and conditioning. Too dry, and bran shatters, flour is dark, and milling is hard. Too wet, and wheat sticks to rollers, molds, and yields poor flour. You need to measure moisture accurately and control it. In Africa, where humidity varies from desert to rainforest, you must check moisture daily.

Use a moisture meter. The best is an electronic meter with a probe that you push into a wheat sample. They cost $100â$300. Cheaper options: a drying oven (weigh 10 g wheat, dry at 130Â°C for 1 hour, reweighâloss is moisture). Or a simple salt test: mix 10 g wheat with 20 g dry salt, shake, and if salt clumps, moisture is above 14%. For accuracy, calibrate your meter monthly with a known sample.

Take samples from different parts of the binâtop, middle, bottom. Moisture varies. Test at least 3 samples and average. Before cleaning, test incoming wheat. If above 14%, dry it first. Spread wheat in thin layers (5 cm) in sun for 2â4 hours, stir every 30 minutes. In humid areas, use a mechanical dryer with low heat (40â50Â°C). Never dry above 60Â°Câit damages gluten.

During tempering, calculate water to add: (Target moisture â Current moisture) Ã Weight of wheat / (100 â Target moisture). Example: 100 kg wheat at 12% moisture, target 16%. Water = (16-12) Ã 100 / (100-16) = 4 Ã 100 / 84 = 4.76 liters. Add this amount. After rest, measure again. If moisture is 15% instead of 16%, add more water: (16-15) Ã 100 / (100-16) = 1.19 liters. Mix and rest 2 hours.

Control moisture in the mill: keep bags sealed, store wheat in dry place, and avoid milling in rain. In coastal Africa, use dehumidifiers or air conditioners in storage. Train workers to record moisture every batch. A simple notebook works. If moisture is off by 1%, flour yield drops by 2â3%. So measure, adjust, and measure again. Good moisture control means consistent flour and happy bakers.

lessons.title: Impact of Conditioning on Milling Performance
lessons.body:
Conditioning directly affects how well your mill runs and how much flour you get. Properly conditioned wheat mills faster, uses less power, and gives higher yield of clean flour. Poor conditioning causes roller wear, clogged screens, and dark flour. In Africa, where energy costs are high, good conditioning saves money.

When wheat is tempered right, bran becomes leathery and endosperm becomes soft. The roller mill breaks the wheat cleanly: bran stays in large flakes, endosperm crushes into flour. You get less bran powder in flour, so flour is whiter and has better baking quality. If wheat is too dry, bran shatters into tiny pieces that mix with flourâyour flour ash content rises. Ash is a measure of bran contamination; target below 0.6% for white flour. If too wet, wheat sticks to rollers, causing uneven grinding and blockages.

Conditioning also affects sifting. Dry bran sifts easily; wet bran clogs screens. In a typical African mill, a 1% increase in wheat moisture (within target range) can increase flour yield by 1â2%. But over 17% moisture, yield drops because wheat gums up. Power consumption: milling dry wheat uses more energy because it is harder. Proper conditioning can reduce energy use by 10â15%.

Test your conditioning: after tempering, take 100 g wheat and mill it in a small laboratory mill. Sift and weigh flour. Calculate yield: flour weight / wheat weight Ã 100. Good yield for hard wheat is 72â75%. Also check bran: it should come off in large pieces, not powder. If bran is powdery, wheat was too dryâadd more water and rest longer. If bran is sticky and clogs, too wetâreduce water or rest time.

Adjust conditioning for different wheat types. Hard wheat needs more water and longer rest. Soft wheat needs less. In hot climates, rest time is shorter because water absorbs faster. Keep records: wheat type, moisture before and after, rest time, mill settings, yield, and flour ash. After a few batches, you will know the best recipe for your wheat. Good conditioning is the difference between a profitable mill and a struggling one.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Cleaning and Conditioning Issues
lessons.body:
Even with good equipment and methods, problems happen. This lesson helps you diagnose and fix common issues in wheat cleaning and conditioning. Use a systematic approach: check wheat first, then machines, then settings. Keep a logbook of problems and solutions.

Problem: Stones in cleaned wheat. Cause: destoner not working. Check: air flow (increase if low), deck angle (adjust), feed rate (reduce if too high), screen holes (clean if blocked). In Africa, dusty air clogs destoner screensâclean daily. If stones still pass, install a second destoner or a gravity separator.

Problem: Metal pieces in wheat. Cause: magnetic separator weak or missing. Check: magnet strength (test with a nail), clean metal particles off magnet daily. If magnet is weak, replace it. Also install a metal detector before the mill.

Problem: Wheat too wet after tempering. Cause: too much water added or short rest. Check: moisture meter calibration. If meter is wrong, you add wrong water. Recalibrate. If water was correct, extend rest time or add dry wheat to blend. Never mill wet wheatâit clogs rollers.

Problem: Wheat too dry after tempering. Cause: not enough water or long storage. Check: initial moisture (maybe lower than thought). Add more water, mix, rest 2 hours. If in dry climate, cover bins to prevent evaporation.

Problem: Flour dark with bran specks. Cause: poor conditioning (bran shattered) or worn rollers. Check: wheat moisture (should be 15.5â16.5% for hard wheat). If low, add water and rest. Check roller gapsâif too tight, bran breaks. Adjust to recommended setting.

Problem: Mill clogging. Cause: wheat too wet or screens torn. Check: moisture (if >17%, dry wheat). Check screens for holes or sticky buildupâclean or replace. Reduce feed rate if motor overloads.

Problem: Low flour yield. Cause: many factorsâpoor cleaning (stones damage rolls), wrong moisture, worn rolls. Check each step. Start with cleaning: if impurities >2%, improve cleaning. Then check moisture. Then check roll gaps and sharpness. Keep records to spot trends. In Africa, power fluctuations can affect motorsâuse stabilizers. Train staff to report problems early. Fix small issues before they become big breakdowns.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of wheat cleaning?
options: A) To remove impurities that damage equipment and reduce flour quality
D) To make wheat easier to store
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes stones, metal, and other foreign matter that can damage mills and contaminate flour.

quiz.q: Which machine uses air to lift light materials like chaff?
quiz.explanation: An aspirator uses an upward air stream to separate light impurities from wheat.

quiz.q: What is the target moisture range for hard wheat before milling?
quiz.explanation: Hard wheat is tempered to 15.5â16.5% moisture for optimal milling.

quiz.q: How long should hard wheat rest after adding water during tempering?
quiz.explanation: Hard wheat needs 12â24 hours of rest for water to penetrate evenly.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a destoner?
options: B) To separate stones from wheat by density
quiz.explanation: A destoner uses vibration and air to separate heavy stones from lighter wheat.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of poor conditioning?
options: A) Large bran flakes after milling
C) Dark flour with bran specks
quiz.explanation: Dark flour with bran specks indicates bran shattered, often due to wheat being too dry.

quiz.q: What should you do if wheat is too wet after tempering?
options: B) Add dry wheat to blend or let it dry
quiz.explanation: Adding dry wheat or drying reduces moisture to the target level.

quiz.q: What is the recommended air speed for an aspirator?
options: A) Just enough to lift trash but not good wheat
quiz.explanation: Air speed should be adjusted so light trash is removed without losing good wheat.

quiz.q: How often should you clean the air filter on an aspirator in dusty conditions?
quiz.explanation: Dusty African conditions require daily cleaning to maintain air flow.

quiz.q: What is the formula to calculate water to add for tempering?
options: A) (Target â Current) Ã Weight / (100 â Target)
quiz.explanation: This formula accounts for the final moisture basis and gives accurate water addition.

quiz.q: Which wheat type needs more water and longer rest?
quiz.explanation: Hard wheat has a denser endosperm and requires more water and time to temper.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended temperature for warm tempering water?
quiz.explanation: Water at 40â50Â°C speeds penetration but higher temperatures damage gluten.

quiz.q: What does a moisture meter measure?
quiz.explanation: A moisture meter determines the percentage of water in a wheat sample.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test for moisture above 14%?
quiz.explanation: Mixing wheat with dry salt: if salt clumps, moisture is likely above 14%.

quiz.q: How can you reduce wheat moisture before cleaning in humid areas?
options: B) Use a mechanical dryer at 40â50Â°C
quiz.explanation: Mechanical drying with low heat removes excess moisture without damaging gluten.

quiz.q: What is the target ash content for white flour?
quiz.explanation: Low ash indicates less bran contamination and whiter flour.

quiz.q: How does proper conditioning affect energy consumption in milling?
quiz.explanation: Tempered wheat is softer and easier to mill, reducing power needs.

quiz.q: What is a sign that wheat was too dry during milling?
options: A) Bran comes off in large flakes
quiz.explanation: Dry bran shatters into powder, contaminating flour.

quiz.q: What should you check if stones are found in cleaned wheat?
options: B) Destoner air flow, deck angle, and feed rate
quiz.explanation: Destoner settings directly affect stone removal efficiency.

quiz.q: How often should you test the magnetic separator?
quiz.explanation: Daily checks ensure the magnet is clean and strong enough to catch metal.

quiz.q: What causes mill clogging?
options: B) Wheat too wet or torn screens
quiz.explanation: Wet wheat sticks to rollers and screens; torn screens let large particles through.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rest time for soft wheat?
quiz.explanation: Soft wheat requires less rest than hard wheat, typically 6â12 hours.

quiz.q: What is the first step in troubleshooting a cleaning problem?
options: B) Check the wheat and then the machine settings
quiz.explanation: Systematic checks start with incoming wheat quality and then machine adjustments.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a magnetic separator?
options: B) Remove iron and steel pieces
quiz.explanation: Magnetic separators attract and hold metal contaminants.

quiz.q: How can you prevent evaporation during tempering in dry climates?
quiz.explanation: Covers reduce moisture loss to dry air.

quiz.q: What is the typical flour yield for hard wheat after proper conditioning?
quiz.explanation: Good conditioning and milling yield 72â75% flour from hard wheat.

quiz.q: What should you do if flour is dark with bran specks?
options: B) Check wheat moisture and roller gaps
quiz.explanation: Dark flour often results from dry wheat or worn roller settings.

quiz.q: What is a common weed seed that is similar in size to wheat?
quiz.explanation: Wild oats are similar in size to wheat and require specific screens for removal.

quiz.q: How often should you grease bearings on cleaning equipment?
quiz.explanation: Weekly greasing keeps bearings running smoothly and prevents breakdowns.

quiz.q: What is the target moisture for soft wheat before milling?
quiz.explanation: Soft wheat is tempered to 14.5â15.5% moisture for optimal milling.
